summary:
We developed HYPERION-MDA, an onboard medical software architecture that solves three critical failure modes in deep space crew health monitoring: baseline physiology drift in microgravity, exercise induced false alarms, and uncertainty from stale manual exams during 20-minute Mars communication blackouts.

Our solution implements a 5-layer deterministic pipeline:

--(1) Individualized Multi-Modal Fusion: Aligns 1 Hz wearable waveforms (HR, HRV, 3-axis acceleration ENMO, ECG kurtosis), NASA OSDR (OSD-575) lab assays, NOAA/NASA GOES radiation feeds, and 3 crew tools—a millisecond click reaction timer (PVT), an ocular ultrasound caliper (ONSD mm for SANS), and a vitals/glucose logger—using personal resting Z-scores (zᵢ,ₜ) and an exponential staleness decay mask (τₘ,ₜ = e⁻ᵞᵐᵟᵗᵐ).

--(2) Privacy-Preserving Personalized Federated Core: Benchmarks participant-separated scikit-learn baselines against a LayerNorm PyTorch residual network trained across 4 habitat silos (Station, Transit, Lunar Base, Rover) using Flower, Opacus (ε, δ)-DP-SGD, and a Cosine-Median radiation bit-flip filter.

--(3-5) 3-Stage Deterministic Trust Gate & S0–S4 Router: Regresses out physical exertion (ENMO) and cabin CO₂ to block exercise false cardiac alarms (Gate 2), uses Split Conformal bounds and MC-Dropout uncertainty (U(m)) to prompt the single fastest confirmatory self-exam when data is stale (Gate 3), and anchors store-and-forward Flight Surgeon escalations to a SHA-256 (HealthAudit.sol) audit chain.
details:
1. What Is the Problem?

Today on the International Space Station, astronauts have fast internet and doctors on Earth watching their vital signs live. However, on future Moon and Mars missions, radio signals take up to 20 minutes each way, and communication can drop completely.

Standard health monitors fail in deep space for three practical reasons:

  • Example 1 — False Alarms During Daily Exercise: Astronauts must exercise about 2 hours every day so they do not lose bone and muscle. When an astronaut pedals hard on an exercise bike, their heart rate reaches 150+ bpm. A basic threshold monitor thinks they are having a medical emergency and rings a false alarm.
  • Example 2 — Space Changes Normal Body Baselines: In microgravity (0g0g), body fluids shift toward the head, and normal resting heart rate or blood sugar shifts slightly. Fixed Earth hospital cutoffs do not fit an astronaut after weeks in space.
  • Example 3 — Mixing Fast Sensors with Old Manual Checks: A smart shirt records heart rate every second, but an eye ultrasound or reaction test is only done once every few days. Guessing a medical risk from a 3-day-old check can cause wrong alerts.

2. Our Proposed Solution: HYPERION-MDA

We built HYPERION-MDA, an offline-first medical web workstation that runs locally inside the spacecraft. It combines continuous wearable sensors, cabin environment readings, and quick crew self-checks into an interactive 6-organ human body view (Brain/Eyes, Heart, Immune/Radiation, Metabolism, Bone/Kidney, and Sleep/Mood) across 4 space habitats (Space Station, Transit Spacecraft, Lunar Base, and Surface Rover).

3. How Does It Work?

  1. Personal Baselines & Data Freshness Timer: Instead of comparing an astronaut to fixed Earth averages, the system compares each measurement to the astronaut’s own 14-day resting average (Z-score). It also attaches a mathematical freshness timer (τ=e−λΔtτ=e−λΔt) to every input so the system knows whether a manual check was done 5 minutes ago or 2 days ago.
  2. Three Interactive Crew Self-Check Tools:
    • Mouse Click Reaction Timer (PVT): Measures reaction speed in milliseconds to check fatigue and mental sharpness.
    • Ocular Ultrasound Caliper (ONSD): Measures the width of the optic nerve behind the eye (in millimeters) to check for spaceflight eye swelling (SANS).
    • Keyboard Vitals Logger: Logs blood pressure, blood sugar, temperature, water intake, sleep hours, and mood.
  3. 3-Stage Deterministic Safety Gate (Stopping False Alarms):
    • Gate 1 (Sensor Quality Check): Blocks noisy signal spikes if a sensor strap slips.
    • Gate 2 (Exercise Filter): Checks body movement (ENMO acceleration) and cabin CO2CO2​. If heart rate is high because the astronaut is exercising, the system labels it as normal exertion and blocks the false alarm.
    • Gate 3 (Ask Before Alarming): If the model sees a possible risk (for example, high cabin CO2CO2​and slower clicks) but the eye ultrasound is 48 hours old, it pauses the alarm (S2 Hold) and asks the astronaut to do the single quickest check to be sure.
  4. Delayed Flight Surgeon Outbox (S0–S4 Workflow): If the new check confirms a real issue, the app shows simple, step-by-step instructions to the crew (S3) and saves a summary packet in a local SQLite outbox (S4) that automatically syncs with Earth doctors when radio contact returns.

4. Why We Chose Each Technical Component (And How We Handled Trade-Offs)

  • Why Simple Baselines + a Small Neural Network (~12,000 Parameters)?
    Human spaceflight datasets have very few subjects. Large deep-learning models easily overfit small datasets and require heavy GPUs. We first trained simple scikit-learn baselines (LogisticRegression and RandomForest) separated strictly by participant ID, and then built a compact 42-input PyTorch residual network using LayerNorm. It is only ~48 KB in size and runs in under 15 milliseconds on a standard laptop CPU without internet.
  • Why Federated Learning (Flower) and Differential Privacy (Opacus)?
    Real-life reason: Imagine 2 astronauts are in a Lunar Base and 2 are on an Orbiting Station. Sending raw, second-by-second heart waveforms between habitats wastes narrow radio bandwidth and shares private medical records. Federated Learning lets each habitat train the model locally on its own computer and share only tiny math weight updates (~48 KB). We added Differential Privacy (Opacus) so raw health numbers cannot be reverse-engineered from those weights, and a Cosine-Median filter so if space radiation causes a bit-flip error on one habitat's computer, the corrupted update is rejected.
  • Why Blockchain / SHA-256 Audit Hashing Even Though Blockchains Add Inefficiency?
    Public blockchains use heavy mining, run slowly, and waste power—which is a bad fit for a spacecraft. Also, putting private medical data on a blockchain is unsafe.
    How we solved this: We never run heavy proof-of-work mining and never put raw health numbers on-chain. Instead, whenever an alert (S3/S4) or Flight Surgeon acknowledgement happens, our backend creates a tiny 32-byte SHA-256 hash (a digital fingerprint) in less than 1 millisecond and links it to the previous hash in SQLite (and an optional local HealthAudit.sol smart contract).
    Why is it useful? Just like an airplane’s "black box" flight recorder, if a medical emergency happens during a 20-minute Mars blackout, doctors and mission review boards get tamper-proof verification of what the sensors read →→ what the software recommended →→ when the Flight Surgeon signed off, with almost zero extra CPU cost and full medical privacy.

5. Benefits & Intended Impact

  • For Space Missions: Reduces crew alarm fatigue during daily exercise, helps non-doctor astronauts take the right action during 20-minute communication blackouts, and keeps medical data private across habitats.
  • For Earth Healthcare: The exact same offline, low-bandwidth software can be used in rural health clinics, submarines, cargo ships, and Antarctic stations, where staff have basic wearables and portable ultrasound probes but unreliable internet access to specialist doctors.

6. Tools, Coding Languages & Software Used

  • Languages: Python, TypeScript, SQL, Solidity
  • Backend & Storage: FastAPI, SQLite, Pydantic
  • Machine Learning & Signal Processing: PyTorch, scikit-learn, SciPy, NumPy, Flower (Federated Learning), Opacus (Differential Privacy)
  • Frontend UI: React, Vite, Tailwind CSS
  • Audit & Testing: Python hashlib (SHA-256 chain), Hardhat/Solidity (HealthAudit.sol), Pytest, Vitest

7. Research & References Used

  1. NASA Human Research Program (HRP) — 5 Hazards & Risks of Human Spaceflight: Used to map the 5 RIDGE hazards (Radiation, Isolation, Distance/20-min delay, Gravity, Hostile Closed Environments) and the 6 organ domains, including Spaceflight-Associated Neuro-ocular Syndrome (SANS).
  2. Canadian Space Agency (CSA) — Bio-Monitor & Vascular Series Research: Used to design our wearable sensor channels and account for spaceflight arterial stiffening and subclinical insulin resistance (elevated fasting blood sugar in microgravity).
  3. Canadian Space Agency (CSA) — Radiation Monitoring: Used to design our solar storm shelter triage protocol.
  4. NASA Open Science Data Repository (OSD-575): Real human spaceflight longitudinal lab and biomarker assay panels used in our verified data pipeline.
  5. NOAA / NASA GOES Proton Flux API & PhysioNet Wearable Waveforms: Used for real satellite radiation telemetry (pfu) and Leave-One-Participant-Out (n=8) wearable physiological model testing.
